commentary.bottom_line: Nineteen sources endorse a standardized plain-language model card for each AI tool, including CHAI frameworks that list it as a requirement and draft FDA guidance that recommends model card content, but no supplied study tests whether model cards improve clinician or governance decisions. The recommendation rests on consensus and regulatory expectation rather than on measured effects.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests model cards, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The endorsements consist of frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, which express expert agreement but do not measure whether documentation changes tool selection, clinician use, or patient outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, this body of support cannot be rated for certainty of effect.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions states that sponsors should include model card information even without the model card structure. CHAI playbooks require a model information sheet covering data sources, training methods, and risk. These documents suggest that model cards may become an expected element of submissions and procurement, independent of outcome evidence.

Several endorsements ask that model cards report performance across patient subgroups and known biases. No supplied study examines whether such reporting leads organizations to detect or correct performance gaps affecting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so any equity benefit remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare governance and clinician decisions with and without standardized model cards, measuring whether the cards change adoption choices, detection of limitations, appropriate use, and patient outcomes, and at what cost to developers and deployers to maintain them across versions.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that model card subgroup reporting will surface performance problems for their patients without local validation.
